newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ESKOM DEBTORS TO VET S.AFRICAN POWER PLAN.
newsitem.headline: ESKOM DEBTORS TO VET S.AFRICAN POWER PLAN.

text.p: A new plan to rescue South Africa's ambitious electrification programme would have to be approved by electricity utility Eskom's local and foreign backers, a parliamentary committee heard on Wednesday.

Department of Minerals and Energy deputy director Wolsey Barnard told the minerals and energy committee that this would involve "sensitive" negotiations as many of the local authorities with whom Eskom could team up with were in serious financial diffculties.

South Africa has set itself the target of electrifying 450,000 houses a year but the programme is being threatened by the fact that many local authorities, which act as distributors, are not financially viable.
The department has developed a new model to divide the country into about five regional electricity distributors (REDs), which would be joint ventures between Eskom and local authorities.

The joint ventures would probably take the form of public companies and the municipalities and Eskom could either exchange their assets for shares in the company, or lease their assets to the company.

In Eskom's case, its assets have largely been funded through government guaranteed loans from local and foreign financial institutions and Barnard said their approval for any new structure would have to be obtained.

"So if we get clarification on the structure, on the ownership and control (of the company), with that package we can...go to the lenders and say this is what we want to engage in, will you accept this?" he told Reuters.
"If they will not accept it, then we will have to look at what will be acceptable for them."
Eskom has taken out loans worth billions of rand at home and abroad to fund electrification in South Africa.
Barnard said that because of the non-payment of electricity bills, poor service and the loss of skills, most municipalities were in dire financial straits.
Eskom was also being asked on an almost daily basis to help local authorities sort out technical problems.
"There are serious problems with the financial health of the municipalities and it is harming the electricity industry," he said.

Although municipalities earned about two billion rand in profits from the sale of electricity throughout the country last year, about 50 percent of this was earned by the country's five major cities. The others did not have enough consumers to build up surpluses and often used what they did have to cross-subsidise other services.

The department had suggested that municipalities should be able to charge a tax on electricity to help fund electrification programmes, but that this should last only until the programmes were completed.
Barnard said these and other suggestions would be discussed at a special workshop in Pretoria on August 22 and it was hoped that the new structures would be in place within a year.
Any structure decided on would have to have the full support of all stakeholders if it was to succeed, he said.
